stories.title: The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation
stories.headline: The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation
stories.summary: For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity.
stories.expanded:
For the last decade, the datacenter industry has been a quiet engine of the digital economy. It was a background utility that just worked. However, datacenters are no longer passive consumers of electricity.

They are becoming active participants in energy generation, storage, and grid management through behind-the-meter infrastructure. This is being driven by the explosive rise of AI and a manufacturing renaissance. Power demand is growing again, increasing an average of 2.

1 percent annually over the past five years, with datacenters emerging as a dominant driver of long-term growth. Electric Power Research Institute projects that datacenters could consume as much as 17 percent of U. electricity by 2030 , more than triple their current 4-5 percent share.

stories.title: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
stories.headline: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
stories.summary: AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell. Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse. The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior , is back with another report about holiday toy trouble.
stories.expanded:
AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell. Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse. The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior , is back with another report about holiday toy trouble.

They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging. Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok ( no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report.

As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear.

stories.title: MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS
stories.headline: MPs ask what the break clause was for as Palantir wins two more years in the NHS
stories.summary: Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years. Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal , awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers.
stories.expanded:
Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years. Health minister James Frith told MPs on Monday that the current contract would continue until March 2029 as the government procures a new version of the Federated Data Platform (FDP). The existing Palantir-led deal , awarded in 2023, has a maximum value of £330 million and includes other suppliers.

Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit. " Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic.

Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits . Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision.

stories.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
stories.headline: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
stories.summary: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.
stories.expanded:
A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.

2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote .

Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree. " He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery.

stories.title: Website owners thumb their noses at EU privacy rules, researcher finds
stories.headline: Website owners thumb their noses at EU privacy rules, researcher finds
stories.summary: The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher's investigation. Forensic data analysis , published by Alexander Hanff, an attorney, computer scientist, and occasional contributor to The Register , with the support of SOMI (Stichting Onderzoek Marktinformatie), a Netherlands-based privacy group, details the dubious data flow. From October 1 to 3, 2026, Hanff took a clean Google Chrome browser profile and measured what happens when the browser loads the 100 most visited English-language websites for five minutes, without any consent banner interaction.
stories.expanded:
The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher's investigation. Forensic data analysis , published by Alexander Hanff, an attorney, computer scientist, and occasional contributor to The Register , with the support of SOMI (Stichting Onderzoek Marktinformatie), a Netherlands-based privacy group, details the dubious data flow. From October 1 to 3, 2026, Hanff took a clean Google Chrome browser profile and measured what happens when the browser loads the 100 most visited English-language websites for five minutes, without any consent banner interaction.

At these 100 sites, visits were made to 265 pages – the home page, the privacy page, and the cookie notice when available – which resulted in 518,770 privacy events without any consent. All 100 sites produced what the report characterizes as Tier 1 events – interception, exfiltration, or high-entropy fingerprinting (a total of 14,675). Tier 2 consists of storage on the device, capturing device characteristics, and script loads without consent (284,463 events recorded).

Tier 3 includes protocol mechanisms and passive reads used for tracking (219,632 events). The median website triggered 2,695 events, for a total of 28,695 events deemed high or critical. 4 percent of the servers contacted during this process were on networks outside the European Economic Area (EEA).

stories.title: REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant
stories.headline: REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant
stories.summary: Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion. AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis.
stories.expanded:
Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion. AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis.

This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs. A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them. One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi.

We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed. In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build.

stories.title: Optimizely hack turns world's biggest websites into malware dispensers
stories.headline: Optimizely hack turns world's biggest websites into malware dispensers
stories.summary: Some of the world's most popular websites spent Monday serving malware to visitors after crooks found a way into a piece of software used to A/B test web pages. Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, identified malicious JavaScript being served by websites belonging to at least 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce, HSB, and TalkTalk. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software.
stories.expanded:
Some of the world's most popular websites spent Monday serving malware to visitors after crooks found a way into a piece of software used to A/B test web pages. Scott Helme, a security researcher at Report URI, identified malicious JavaScript being served by websites belonging to at least 178 organizations, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom, IKEA, Salesforce, HSB, and TalkTalk. All have one thing in common: they use Optimizely's Web Experimentation software.

Optimizely allows businesses to tweak the content and layout of their websites without changing the underlying site code. Unfortunately, someone other than its paying customers figured out how to do just that. The attackers abused a feature that allows Optimizely customers to add their own JavaScript to web pages.

The malicious code was distributed alongside the legitimate stuff from Optimizely's own content delivery network, giving customers little reason to suspect anything was amiss. Optimizely has since confirmed that the criminals exploited a vulnerability, dubbed "OPTIMJACK" by researchers, in the sign-up process for its experimentation software, adding that it had patched the hole, removed the offending code, revoked tokens, and notified affected customers. "Earlier today, Optimizely identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects,” the company said.

stories.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
stories.headline: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
stories.summary: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1. 8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.
stories.expanded:
Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1. 8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.

Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap.

Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period.

stories.title: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take  off with license data of Uber drivers
stories.headline: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take  off with license data of Uber drivers
stories.summary: Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.
stories.expanded:
Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.

Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week . According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7.

Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier.

stories.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
stories.headline: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
stories.summary: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions.
stories.expanded:
Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions.

What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public. " Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

stories.title: 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer
stories.headline: 350 tech jobs hammered as TCS takes over work at iconic Australian retailer
stories.summary: Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error.
stories.expanded:
Indian tech giant Tata Consultancy Services has a new client, iconic Australian retailer Bunnings Warehouse which has made a third of its IT department redundant. Bunnings is Australia’s equivalent of big box hardware retailers Home Depot and B&Q and earlier today advised its IT teams to attend a town hall meeting. The Register understands the invitation to that meeting was sent twice, after the first effort contained an error.

We hear from staff that the botched invitation was taken as a clue of what was to happen next, namely the announcement of 230 redundancies plus an end to 120 contracted roles. The town hall meeting was not interactive, with a Bunnings rep speaking from a script and not taking questions. Staff whose roles will end then received an email inviting them to a meeting.

Bunnings, whose logo is a hammer, has tried to explain the decision in a statement that says, “We need a technology model and partner that keeps pace with our customers so that we can continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect from us. ” “These changes reflect the way customers are choosing to shop and the increasingly competitive retail environment,” the statement adds, before pointing out “Bunnings is already investing in technology and digital experiences to respond to these changes, earlier this year becoming the first Australian retailer to launch an AI-powered shopping agent using Google's Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience platform through Buddy. ” Some of the TCS workers Bunnings is hiring will work in Australia.

The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1.
stories.expanded:
SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos. The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1.

In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor. Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026.

He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products. In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation.

stories.title: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
stories.headline: Los Alamos boffins to put NextSilicon's Maverick-2 through natural selection in Darwin testbed
stories.summary: The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators.
stories.expanded:
The US Department of Energy (DoE) is deepening its relationship with HPC-first chip startup NextSilicon. During Supercomputing 2026 in Chicago on Monday, the Israeli startup revealed that the agency had deployed its second Maverick-2 cluster in the Darwin testbed at Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL). The deployment comes just six months after Sandia National Laboratories powered on NextSilicon’s first supercomputer, which features 64 nodes and 128 of the company's “runtime-configurable” accelerators.

NextSilicon’s latest DoE system is comparatively smaller, comprising just four accelerators, yet for LANL, the system is arguably more important despite its size. Darwin, LANL’s chief scientist Galen Shipman, tells El Reg is a “long-lived testbed environment where we bring in newer technologies for evaluation. ” “It gives us the ability to work with the technology much more quickly, and integrate it with other components of our architecture in our environment,” he explained.

Smaller systems like the Maverick-2 cluster now deployed in Darwin allow LANL to validate and port a wider array of codebases to the chips, identify problems, and work with NextSilicon to not only address them, but directly influence the capabilities of future chips, Shipman explained. In other words, Los Alamos’ interest in Maverick-2 is the first step toward larger scale deployments of NextSilicon silicon in future DoE supers. For this, hands-on access is kind of important as many of LANL’s most important workloads can’t exactly be run on public systems.
